definition: Acclimate means to become accustomed to a new climate or set of conditions.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word acclimate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know acclimate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: It took the night crew a week to acclimate to the graveyard shift, but soon the 2 a.m. start felt as ordinary as breakfast.
Coping is far weaker than acclimating — you grit your teeth and get through days that still feel foreign, while a person who has acclimated barely notices the same conditions.
Adjusting means making small deliberate changes — a new alarm, a warmer coat — but it stops short of acclimating, where the new conditions finally feel like home.

To adapt is to change your methods, gear, or habits so they fit a new demand; it covers any change made to fit new needs. Acclimate is narrower: you redesign nothing and instead grow used to conditions little by little until they feel normal.

Settling in is the friendly, everyday phrase for getting comfortable somewhere new: unpacking, learning names, finding your favorite seat. Acclimate is more bodily and gradual — your whole system keeps shifting until a once-harsh climate or schedule finally feels normal, whether or not you feel at home yet.

Acclimate is the word for settling into new conditions gradually — an altitude, a schedule, a workplace.
For a one-time tweak, adjust is plainer.
Note how it divides labor with its unit-mate withstand: acclimating changes you until the conditions feel normal; withstanding holds you unchanged against them.

When the orchestra hired Mireille away from her sea-level conservatory, its concert hall stood at three thousand meters.
For the first week she could not finish a phrase without stealing a breath, and climbing the stage stairs left her dizzy.
The conductor told her not to change a thing about her playing — there was nothing to fix, he said; she simply had to acclimate.
So she practiced her usual hours and waited while her body adjusted to the thin air.
By the third week her lungs had stopped keeping score, and by the fourth she noticed the altitude only when visitors gasped on the stairs.
